6.187.m: The Goddess said: / "The glorification of the twelfth chapter has been narrated to me by you; / tell me the exceedingly beautiful glorification of the thirteenth chapter!"

The Lord said:
Listen, O auspicious Śivā, to the ocean of greatness of the thirteenth chapter, / by merely hearing which you will attain supreme delight.
In the southern region is the great river Tuṅgabhadrā; / on its bank is a delightful city named the town of Harihara,
where the blessed god Harihara himself dwells, O goddess, / by whose mere sight the highest good is attained.
In that city there was a twice-born man named Haridīkṣita, / devoted to austerities and Vedic study, learned in scripture, and fully versed in the Vedas.
He had a wife named Durācārā, and such she was by her deeds; / abusive in speech, she never slept with her husband.
Following her own whims, she did not stay even for a moment in her own house; / she drank liquor up to her throat at the doors of the twice-born.
Ever scolding all the relatives of her husband, / she was constantly intoxicated and continually revelling with paramours.
Once, seeing the town crowded here and there with citizens, / she herself made a rendezvous house in a desolate wilderness.
Then, revelling right there with paramours, that cunning woman, / proud of her youth, spent a long time.
Then, while she was dwelling without restraint in that lovely city, / there arrived the spring season, the foremost friend of the god of love on earth,

6.187.s:
āmūlapallavākīrṇaṃ sahakāravikāriṇā
pikānāṃpaṃcamālāpaiḥ punaḥ sajīvitaḥ smaraḥ
6.187.d:
आमूलपल्लवाकीर्णं सहकारविकारिणा
पिकानांपंचमालापैः पुनः सजीवितः स्मरः
6.187.m: strewn with tender sprouts down to the roots by blooming mango trees; / by the cooing of cuckoos in the fifth note, the god of love was revived again.
The forest trees were swayed by the Malaya breezes slowly creeping forth, / carrying away the fragrance of gleaming campaka flowers.
It was embellished all around with the buzz of bees / having their feast on the wine of the fragrance of fully blown jasmine.
Smiling with lakes bright, pleasing, and fragrant, / it was made manifest by ponds with flocks of resting swans.
The earth was adorned with diverse trees having thick foliage, / which sheltered fawns comfortably seated in their deep shade.
In that springtime, that delighted wanton woman / saw the moonlight at night that gives joy to the world,
from which sprays of nectar fell from the tips of the beaks of darting cakora birds, / filled with torrents of nectar flowing from melting moonstones,
whose clusters of rays thickened in the center of blooming blossoms, / which embraced the sky with the surging billows of the ocean,
which was a pair of shears at the throat of unchaste women for the great lion of Kama, / and clever at tearing apart the dense mass of darkness,
which held frost within, having whitened and insulted other things, / and gave delight to youth on account of the contraction of faded day-lotuses,
witnessing the plaintive cries from the mouths of female cakravāka birds, / illuminating the spaces between the directions with the pure luster of strings of pearls.
Then, when that [moonlight] had spread forth filling the ten directions, / that passionate woman, blinded by lust, walked upon the road to the mansion.
Seeing no paramours at night, she broke the bolt of the house, / went outside the town, and went to the rendezvous house.
Her mind bewildered by desire, searching for a lover there, / she did not see anyone in bower after bower and under tree after tree.
Hearing the soft murmurs of her beloved at every step, / she went toward them, sporting where there was a rustling sound.
Hearing the cries of cakravāka birds, mistaking them for the speech of her lover, / she wandered again and again around all the lakes.
Mistaking them for her lover, she awoke the herds of deer / sleeping under the trees, saying with a sigh, “I have arrived!”
She embraced a tree-trunk in the forest, thinking it to be the lord of her life; / and mistaking it for his face, she repeatedly kissed a blown lotus.

Having made useless exertion here and there and not seeing her beloved, / she herself lamented in that forest with various words as if fainting: / “Alas, beloved! Alas, you who are filled with virtues, master of my consciousness!
O handsome one, treasure of good fortune, destiny, and beauty! / Alas, you whose face is like the full moon! Alas, you whose eyes are like long lotus petals!
Alas, beloved, wishing-tree for complete satisfaction and rest in truth! / If you are staying here in a hidden guise out of some anger,
I will appease you, beloved, even by offering my dear life!” / As she was lamenting aloud in this way in every direction out of separation,

6.187.s:
tasyāḥ śrutvāvacaḥ ko'pisuptovyāghraḥ prabuddhavān
kurvanghuraghuradhvānaṃpaśyanpratidiśaṃ ruṣā
6.187.d:
तस्याः श्रुत्वावचः कोऽपिसुप्तोव्याघ्रः प्रबुद्धवान्
कुर्वन्घुरघुरध्वानंपश्यन्प्रतिदिशं रुषा
6.187.m: a sleeping tiger was awakened on hearing her voice. / Making a growling sound, looking toward every direction in rage,
striking the ground with its claws, roaring into the cavern of the sky, / with its tail curved over its back, rising quickly and forcefully,
the tiger leaped forward and went to where that wanton woman was. / Then, seeing him approaching, she thought he was her husband,
and with a mind overwhelmed by love, she stepped forward to stand before him. / Then, blinded by the cruelty of the play of his claws,
she abandoned the suspicion that it was the body of her beloved on hearing his mighty roar. / Even being in such a state, that woman quickly cast aside her confusion and said:
“For what reason, O tiger, have you come here to slay me? / Tell me all this, since you wish to kill me.”
Hearing her words, the tiger of terrible prowess, / pausing for a moment from that meal, said, as if laughing:
“In the southern country there is a river named Malāpahā; / on its bank is a city named Muniparṇā.
There dwells the blessed Maheśvara visibly as Pañcaliṅga. / Having been born as the son of a brāhmaṇa in that city, I dwelt there.
Sacrificing for those not fit to be sacrificed for, eating funeral offerings on the riverbank, / constantly selling the fruit of reciting the Veda out of longing for wealth,
scolding other beggars with harsh words out of greed, / taking unreceivable wealth, and ceaselessly day after day taking what was not given,
deceiving all the people out of eagerness to seize the moment, / after some time I arrived at old age.
Wrinkled, gray-haired, blind, falling down, stumbling in my gait, / my teeth falling out, I remained wholly devoted to accepting gifts.
Taking darbha grass in hand, I went near sacred places, / wandering on every festive occasion out of greed to obtain money.
Then, with my limbs weakened, I went to a certain house of a brāhmaṇa / to eat what had been begged for, and in the middle of it I was bitten on the foot by a dog.
I fainted and instantly fell to the ground; / then, my breath departed, and I entered the womb of a tiger.
I stay here in this forest remembering my past sins. / I do not devour righteous people, sages, virtuous folk, or faithful wives;
rather, I devour sinners, the ill-behaved, and unchaste women. / Therefore, as you are truly an unchaste woman, you are indeed a morsel for me.”
Having spoken thus, tearing her limb from limb with his sharp claws, / she, having taken refuge in a sinful body, was then eaten by him.
the servants of Yama immediately brought her to the city of Saṃyamanī; / and there, by Yama’s command, they quickly cast her
in various ways into terrible pits filled with feces, urine, and blood. / When ten million kalpas had expired, they brought her repeatedly from there
and placed her in Raurava for the duration of a hundred manvantaras. / Then, dragging her along, wretched, crying, looking in all directions,
her hair dishevelled, her limbs broken, they threw her into the mouth of fire. / Thus, having experienced the terrible torments of hell due to sin,
Because of her grave sin, she was born here again in the wombs of dog-cookers. / Then, even in that dog-cooker's house, growing day by day,
she was just as she had been before, entirely under the sway of her previous birth. / Then, after some time, she returned to her own abode,
where the goddess Jṛmbhakā, the mistress of the city of Śiva, resides. / There she saw a pure twice-born named Vāsudeva,
unceasingly reciting the thirteenth chapter of the Gītā. / Then, merely from hearing that, she was freed from her dog-cooker body,
attained a celestial form, and went to the abode of the gods.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter in the Gītā-māhātmya of the Uttarakhaṇḍa in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.

6.188.m: The Lord said: / Next, O Bhavānī, I shall speak for the sake of release from worldly existence. / Listen attentively, O sweet-smiling one, to the fourteenth chapter of the Gītā.
On this earth there is indeed the vast region of Kāśmīra, / and there stands the delightful capital of Sarasvatī,
presiding over which the goddess of speech grants the world of Brahmā. / Although mounted on a swan, Sāvitrī is [served] there even by [kings] bowed low;
resorting to the service of Sarasvatī's lotus-feet with saffron, / where the regions of the sky are made brilliant with [pollen] born from the hollows of swans' wings.
There, ceaselessly among people speaking Sanskrit, / the divine language of the gods is easily obtained.
Where in the morning, by the saffron dust rising from courtyards of homes, / the orb of the moon and the sun has a reddish hue on every side.
There ruled a king named Śauryavarmā, an assemblage of splendor, / who shattered the hosts of his enemies with a flood of rising, radiant arrows.
And on the island of Siṃhala there was a king of leonine valor, / named Vikramavetāla, a treasure-house of the arts as well.
Both gradually increased their mutual friendship / with abundant, unprecedented gifts produced in their respective lands.
Once, having seen a pair of female hounds sent with great affection by Śauryavarmā, / King Vikramavetāla,
sent in return to his friend Śauryavarmā an abundance / of rutting elephants, horses, jeweled ornaments, and chowries.
Once, mounted on a palanquin, fanned with lovely chowries, / with [hounds] held by golden chains, to the sounding din of drums,
taking the pair of hounds, eager for the pleasure of the hunt, / the king went to the outer hunting-ground along with the princes.
When a hare was cornered to place a wager [on its flesh], / a great clamor arose there among the princes.
Then, having made a costly wager with a certain prince of equal age, / the king playfully engaged in sport.
Then, bringing down from the palanquin the female hound proud of her fame, / the king unleashed her straight behind the fleeing hare.
The mighty-armed prince also released his own beloved hound; / he stopped after loudly proclaiming her line of victories.
As this pair of hounds ran with imperceptible speed, / [the hare] sprang forward before the eyes of all the kings.
From utter exhaustion, that hare fell into a great pit; / yet even though fallen, the young hare was not overcome by the hounds.
Then, slowly rising and running, leaping upon it in fury, / the hare, spewing foam, was seized by the king's hound.
Then, somehow leaping and stumbling away, the hare / was caught by the prince's hound at the edge of its neck.
As the men clamored loudly, shouting, "We have completely won!", / [the hare] slipped from the mouth of the hound, who was startled by the tumult.
Then, with streams of blood flowing from a row of fang-wounds, / the hare stayed hidden in a certain patch of ground.

As the king's hound sniffed the ground in fierce anger, / the terrified hare, as soon as it was seen, fled just a cubit away,

Where, having the hollows of tigers' caves in the midst of camphor-plantains, / the breeze blows, kissing the cheeks of Colī women.
Where its eyes were closed by the pollen of blooming screwpine buds, / [and] where deer confidently cast their shade,
where even the monkeys were satiated with coconuts that had fallen down of their own accord / and with ripe mango fruits,
where even lions played with elephant calves, / and serpents entered fearlessly among the feathers of peacocks.
Where inside a hermitage a tranquil twice-born named Vatsa, master of his senses, / lived, continuously reciting the fourteenth chapter [of the Gītā].
There, going to the mud made by the water that washed his disciple's lotus-feet, / [the hare], panting repeatedly with only a remnant of life left, collapsed.
Then, having crossed over worldly existence merely by the touch of that mud, / the hare mounted a celestial aerial chariot and departed to heaven.
Then the hound too, her limbs smeared with a few drops of that mud, / freed from the torment of hunger and thirst, cast off her canine form,
and then, mounting a celestial chariot delightful with divine maidens / and graced by Gandharvas, the hound also went to heaven.
Then the wise disciple named Svakandhara laughed, / wondering in astonishment at the cause of their enmity from a previous birth.
The king also, his eyes smiling with wonder, bowed down / with supreme devotion—an ocean of humility alone—and questioned him:
"Tell me the story, O twice-born: how did this hound and young hare, / born in low wombs and devoid of knowledge, go to heaven?"
The disciple said: / "A twice-born named Vatsa lives in this forest, having subdued his senses, / always reciting the fourteenth chapter of the Gītā.
I am his disciple, O king, skilled in the knowledge of Brahman; / O ruler, I too recite the fourteenth chapter every day.
By rolling in the water from the washing of my lotus-feet, / the hare, along with the hound, has attained heaven, O lord of the earth."
The king said: / "Tell me, O best of the twice-born, for what reason did you laugh? / Thinking respectfully that there is some significant meaning in this, [I ask]."
The disciple said: / "In Mahārāṣṭra there was a great city named Pratyudaka. / There lived a brāhmaṇa named Keśava, the foremost of gamblers.
His wife Vilobhanā was wanton in her conduct. / She was slain in anger by him, accumulating enmity from that lifetime.
Then, through the sin of killing a woman, that twice-born was born as a hare, / and she too, from the sin of deception in that birth, was born as a hound.
They indeed do not forget the enmity practiced in a previous birth, / though they had entered various other wombs at some time.
Reflecting upon all this, the king, filled with faith, / practiced the entire Gītā and attained the supreme state.

6.189.m: The Lord said: / I shall declare [it], O large-eyed daughter of the snowy mountain; / listen attentively to the glorification of the fifteenth chapter of the Gītā.
There was a compassionate king among the Gauḍas named Narasiṃha, / by the edge of whose sword in battle hosts of gods were given offerings.
By the streams of rutting fluid flowing from whose rutting elephants, the earth / could endure the torment of the sun's heat even in the summer season.
Frightened of Indra, rutting elephants sought his protection / and shone like moving mountains.
The mountains, as if respectfully echoing the trumpet calls of rutting elephants, / spoke forth on behalf of the compassionate one who gave them shelter.
Shattered by the pounding of his galloping horses’ hooves, / how is it that the earth did not break into pieces—what a wonder!
While this friend of Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, was upholding the earth, / the Lord of Serpents once more brought to brilliance the Mahābhāṣya.
He had an intelligent [commander], a treasury of the sciences of arms and treatises, / named Śarabhabheruṇḍa, possessing fierce, mighty arms.
In treasury, in horses, in soldiers born of the heroic sentiment, / and in fortifications extremely impassable, he was equal to the king himself.
Once, that wicked man set his mind on ruling the kingdom himself, / having slain the protector of the earth by force, along with his sons.
While he was resolving to accomplish this within a few days out of that desire, / he swiftly died of a cholera affliction.
Passing away after a short time, that sinful soul, because of that deed, / was born in the Sindh country as a splendid horse with a slender belly.
Purchased for a great price by someone who knew the qualities of horses, / he was brought with great care by a son of a vaiśya.
The king, too, after his death, surrounded by grandsons and great-grandsons, / attained old age in the course of time, while still protecting his realm.
That merchant's son arrived to present the horse to the king; / standing there at the king's gate, he awaited an audience with him.
Though already known, that vaiśya was announced by the doorkeeper; / asked by the king, “State your purpose,” he spoke clearly:
“Sire, considering this horse with excellent marks / a jewel of the three worlds, I bought him for a very great, ten-lakh price.”
Then, looking at the faces of his courtiers standing by, / the king ordered the merchant: “Let the horse be brought here.”
Causing the men knowledgeable in the marks of horses to shake their heads [in awe], / and constantly thrilling the hearts of the valiant, the great [steed approached],
As if vomiting his exceedingly bright fame, earned by swift traversal / of the whole undivided earth, in the guise of frothy saliva;
He truly rivaled Uccaiḥśravas by equality of virtues; / exceedingly fiery, he manifested this with his arched neck held proud.
Constantly fanned with moon-white chowries, / he was like Uccaiḥśravas with his breaths stirring the milk-ocean.
Bearing a pair of blue parasols possessing the beauty of dense shade, / he bore the splendor of the peak of the Himalayas kissed by rainclouds.
Frequently lifting his feet as if fire had passed into them from touching the earth’s orb, / and shaking the handsome slope of his neck,
Tearing apart all enemies and proclaiming the fortune of victory, / he made his fame known in all directions with a deep neighing sound.
He was a mass of vital strength, a treasure-trove of swift gaits, / beauty's visible abode, an ocean of auspicious marks.
The horse, brought by the merchant, was viewed by the king / and extensively praised by ministers skilled in the marks of horses.
Having generously given gold to the merchant as desired, / the king swiftly took the horse, filled with boundless joy.
Then, summoning the keeper of horses and carefully instructing him, / the king dismissed the court and entered his inner chambers.
Often questioned on the battlefield by the king, / adorned with a line of scar-calluses from weapon-wounds, resembling pure spirit,
Once, engaging in the sport of hunting out of curiosity, / the king mounted him and entered the forest.
Leaving behind all his soldiers running all around in his rear, / drawn away by deer, he became overcome with thirst.
Then, dismounting from the horse, the king sought water; / tying the horse to the branch of a tree, the king climbed onto a rock.
He then saw half a verse of the fifteenth chapter of the Gītā written down, / blown there by the wind, lying upon a piece of birch bark.
Hearing the line of Gītā syllables as the king read the page, / the horse immediately attained the state of liberation and fell down swiftly.
Then, cutting the knot and removing the saddle, / the king tried to raise the horse, but he did not rise—he was dead.
Then Śarabhabheruṇḍa, addressing the king in a pleasant voice / and mounting a divine celestial vehicle, went to the abode of the gods.
Then, climbing the mountain, [the king] saw an excellent hermitage, / filled with punnāga, plantain, mango, and coconut trees,
With grape arbors, sugarcane plots, areca palms, nāgakesara, and campaka trees, / where young camels and antelopes frolicked and flocks of peacocks danced.
Bowing to a twice-born sage residing within the leaf-hut, / who was free from worldly desires, he inquired with supreme devotion:
“Tell me, by what cause did the horse depart to heaven?” / Hearing the king's words, the twice-born sage spoke these words:
“Having died long ago, he became a horse on account of that sin. / Now half a verse of the fifteenth chapter was written somewhere;
Hearing it as you read it, the horse departed to heaven.” / Surrounded then by his retinue who had arrived there,
Bowing to the twice-born sage, with his hair standing on end [with joy], he departed. / Taking that very leaf on which the words of the Gītā’s fifteenth chapter were written,
The king read it, his eyes blossoming with joy. / Having consecrated his own son along with his ministers, knowing sacred mantras,
Upon the throne, he [enthroned] the one possessing the strength of a lion; and with a purified mind, he attained liberation.

6.190.m: The Lord said: / Hereafter I will declare the greatness of the sixteenth chapter; / listen, O deer-eyed lady who pours forth joy and eager longing!
In the Gurjara territory there is a city named Saurāṣṭrika; / there ruled Khaḍgabāhu, a king like a second moon.
In the ocean, whose interior was perfumed by garlands of the fragrance of his flowers, / Hari slept at ease together with Lakṣmī.
In the courtyard of the sky, particles of the camphor of his fame shine, / scattered by the winds of his enemies’ sighs in the guise of stars.
Enemy kings who have bathed in the holy waters of the edge of his sword / do not return from heaven even today, enchanted by the speech of celestial maidens.
He had a rutting elephant named Arimardana, haughty with rut, / with swarms of humming bees hovering over the stream of his rut-fluid;
Turbid with rut-streams flowing down the flat expanse of his temples, / he shone like a mountain of collyrium with high cascades.
On his body shone chowries bright as moonlight, / like rays of the cool-beamed moon fallen into the interior of a forest.
With the region of his frontal globes radiant with layers of red-lead dust, / he looked like a piece of the sky covered by twilight clouds.
Once, breaking his chains and shackles, / and forcibly smashing his firm iron post, he escaped in the night.
Disregarding out of wrath all the mahouts / with goads flashing at his heels, he smashed down his own stable.
Even though he was being struck on all sides with sharp elephant goads and bamboo rods, / the riders could not frighten him in the least.
Then the king, having heard of this marvel, came there / along with the princes who were skilled in the art of handling elephants.
Approaching, the mighty elephant was seen by the king, / bewildering [all] with fierce fury, having destroyed a line of balconies.
Standing at a great distance, the citizens watched that terrifying beast, / protecting their children in fear, with all other curiosity abandoned.
While the roads were blocked there by people fleeing, / and scented by the droplets from his spray of fierce musth,
a certain twice-born, having bathed, came along that path from a lake, / reciting several verses of the sixteenth chapter of the Gītā.
Though forbidden in many ways by the citizens and by the elephant-drivers,
paying no heed to the elephant, he walked onward from there as [others] fled; / blowing [him] with his breath, enveloping the people and crushing them,
the twice-born touched his temporal lobe wet with musth and emerged unharmed; / then there arose a great wonder beyond the power of speech,
in the mind of the protector of the earth and of the looking citizens. / Then the king, whose eyes were like blooming lotuses, summoned him,
and, dismounting from his mount and bowing, questioned that twice-born:
The king said: / "A great, extraordinary deed was done by you today, O Brahmin! / How did you come out from this elephant that is like the god of death?
What deity do you worship? What mantra do you recite, O master? / And what siddhi is yours? Speak forth, O twice-born!"
The twice-born said: / "Daily, O king, I recite several verses / of the sixteenth chapter of the Gītā. By that are all these accomplishments [wrought]."
Then, abandoning the elephant and full of wonder, the king / took the twice-born and went to his own palace.
Having observed an auspicious moment, and having pleased that best among the twice-born,
with gold coins numbering in the hundreds of thousands, he received the Gītā mantra, / even several verses of the sixteenth chapter of the Gītā.
Then, having studied it diligently with respect and eager curiosity, the king / once went forth outside accompanied by soldiers.
The king himself released that very elephant in rut from the driver, / speaking clearly these words, holding the happiness of the kingdom as nothing;
regarding his life as a blade of grass, the king then entered before the elephant; / grasping his temple-plate wet with unchecked streams of musth,
the king, foremost among the daring, came forth through confidence in the mantra. / As the moon emerges from the mouth of Rāhu, or as a righteous man from the jaws of Death,
or as a holy man emerges from the mouth of a villain, so the king came forth from the elephant. / Having returned to the city, the king anointed his son,
and attained the supreme state by virtue of the sixteenth chapter of the Gītā.

6.191.m: The Lord said: / "The power of the sixteenth chapter has been told. Hear now / clearly, O Śivā, the ocean of the glory of the seventeenth chapter.
Duḥśāsana was the servant of Khaḍgabāhu's son; / coming to capture that elephant, he met death at the elephant's [hands].
Bound by the latent impressions of that, he took birth as an elephant, / and upon hearing the seventeenth chapter of the Gītā, he attained the highest abode."
The goddess said: / "It is heard that Duḥśāsana attained elephant-hood and was liberated. / O auspicious Lord, tell me that in detail, O master!"
The Lord said: / "A certain foolish man, having made a high wager with princes of feudal rulers, / mounted the elephant from there.
Having advanced only a few steps, though stopped by the people, / that fool named Duḥśāsana, uttering haughty words—
then, having heard his words, the elephant became blinded by rage. / With his feet trembling, [Duḥśāsana] fell down before the princes.
Then, as he lay fallen and breathing faintly, the unrestrained elephant, / wrathful like the god of death, uprooted him into the air.
Even though his life had departed, the enraged elephant, / being in musth, scattered his collection of bones to pieces.
Then, having died in due time, he obtained an elephant's womb; / he spent a great deal of time in [the court of] the king of Siṃhala Island.
Because of a deep friendship with King Khaḍgabāhu, / he was sent along the water-route, regarded as a gift for Varuṇa,
and was brought with affection to King Khaḍgabāhu by Jayadeva. / Remembering his own past birth, and seeing his relatives and brothers,
he spent only a few days in great sorrow, / and stayed quietly in the house of Khaḍgabāhu, revealing nothing.
Once, being pleased by the completion of a riddle verse, / [the king] gave that elephant as a gift to a certain poet.
That elephant was then sold by that poet, who feared the trouble of disease, / to the ruler of the earth of Mālava for one hundred [pieces].
When some time had passed, although looked after with effort, / the elephant became about to die, afflicted with an incurable fever.

The elephant would not smell cold water, nor take a mouthful [of food]; / nor did he sleep in comfort; he merely shed tears. / Then the protector of the earth, told of this circumstance by the elephant-keepers,
having heard it, came to where the feverish elephant was. / Seeing the king, the elephant, whose feverish torment was completely dispelled,
spoke words that produced wonder in the world: / 'O King, knower of all scriptures, ocean of royal statecraft,
vanquisher of multitudes of enemies, beloved of the feet of Murāri! / What use are medicines? Enough of physicians! What use are charities? What use are chanters?
Bring a Brahmin who recites the seventeenth chapter of the Gītā; / by him, this disease of mine will be appeased—there is no doubt of this.'
As instructed by the elephant, so the ruler of men acted; / then, casting off the state of being an elephant, Duḥśāsana was liberated.
When water consecrated with mantras by that Brahmin was sprinkled on his head, / the protector of the earth saw that Duḥśāsana mounted
on a divine aerial chariot, possessing the brilliance of Indra.
The king said: / 'What caste do you belong to? What nature do you have? Tell me what your conduct was. / By what action were you born an elephant? How did you come here?'
Questioned by the king, that liberated one, standing on the aerial chariot, / recounted his own story in steadfast words, as it had happened, step by step.
Reciting the seventeenth chapter of the Gītā, Naravarman, / the king of Mālava, became liberated after a very short time.

6.192.m: Pārvatī said: / 'The greatness of the seventeenth chapter has been spoken by you, O Śiva; / please proclaim now the glory of the eighteenth chapter.'
The Lord said: / 'Listen, O daughter of the mountain, to the holy glorification of the eighteenth chapter, / which brings about the bliss of pure consciousness, the best of the Vedas,
the essence of all scriptures, an elixir when reaching the ears, / devoted to tearing apart the net of the torments of saṃsāra,
the supreme secret of perfected beings, capable of uprooting ignorance, / the consciousness of the enemy of Kaiṭabha, foremost, the supreme state.'
the root of the creeper of discernment, removing the stain of lust and anger, / bringing peace to the minds of the gods headed by Indra;
the source of delight to great yogins headed by Sanaka, / confounding the roars of the servants of Time merely by its recitation;
eradicating the root of the hundred and eight afflictions— / there is no secret higher than this, O [goddess] of the swan's gait,
removing the threefold torment, destroying the great sins. / As I am eternal among the measures of time, as the cow of plenty is among beasts,
as Vyāsa is among chief sages, the knower of Brahman among the Vyāsas, / as Indra is among the dwellers of heaven, and the Preceptor is the best among the leaders of gods,
as nectar is the best of liquids, renowned in all the worlds, / as Kailāsa is among mountains, as Indra is among heaven-dwellers,
as Puṣkara is the most sacred of pilgrimage places, as the lotus is among flowers, / as Arundhatī is among devoted wives throughout the worlds,
as the horse sacrifice is among sacrifices, as Nandana is among pleasure-gardens, / as Vīrabhadra, my follower, is among all the Rudras,
as the gift of land is among gifts, as the Gautamī is among rivers, / as a sanctuary of Hari is celebrated in the world for sacred duties and rites,
just so is the glorification of the eighteenth chapter, supreme over the worlds. / Listen with devotion, O Pārvatī, to this holy narrative therein,
merely by hearing which a living being is freed from sins. / On the peak of Mount Meru stands the delightful city of Amarāvatī,
fashioned in ancient times by Viśvakarman for my delight, / endowed with endless virtues, attended by ten million gods,
possessing an abundance of splendor, celebrated as if it were the knowledge of Brahman in person; / where wish-granting palaces are built of wish-fulfilling stones,
shining triumphantly on the peak of Meru up to the realm of the four-faced [Brahmā]; / where Puloman's daughter, seated comfortably beneath the shade of the wish-fulfilling tree,
listens to the songs of the wives of Gandharvas sung with melodious voices; / where sits the foe of Vala, along with the gods, who severed the lives of the Daityas
whose surges of blood turned the celestial river red; / where the dwellers of heaven, emaciated by hunger,
ever remembering the taste of ancient nectar, sip every day the lunar digit. / In that city, which resembles final liberation, there was once [Indra] of a hundred sacrifices,
endowed with fortune, accompanied by Śacī, served by all the gods. / Once, as he was seated at ease, he saw an extraordinary person approaching,
having a thousand eyes, attended by the messengers of Viṣṇu. / Thereupon Indra, overpowered by his radiance,
fell swiftly from his jeweled throne down into the assembly hall. / When he had departed from his throne, the attendants of Hari
bound the diadem of supreme sovereignty over the host of gods [upon the newcomer]. / Then, while divine kettledrums resounded, Puloman's daughter
swiftly ascended the left lap of that consecrated Great Indra. / Then, as gods celebrated the praises of heaven, filled with joy,
the celestial women waved lustrations over the gods with divine jewels. / Thereupon the ṛṣis gave blessings according to the Vedas;
crowds of apsarases headed by Rambhā danced before him; / and Gandharvas sang songs of joyous celebration with charming utterances.
Seeing this new Indra enjoyed with numerous festivities / without having performed a hundred sacrifices, Śakra was filled with wonder:
“No ponds were made by me along the road, nor were any constructed; / no great trees giving rest to travelers were planted [by him].
Ah, never was the god Tripurabhairava seen; / nor was the goddess Madālasā residing at Nidhivāsa worshipped;
nor was the wielder of the bow Śārṅga residing at Meghaṃkara seen; / no bath was taken at Viraja, nor did he go to the city of Kāśī;
Narahari dwelling in Devavāṭikā was not seen in person; / Eraṇḍaviṣṇu and Heraṃba were never worshipped;
Reṇukā residing in Mātāpura was never beheld; / nor was the goddess dwelling in Dānāpura worshipped with devotion;
Tryambaka the three-linga god was not seen with devotion in Tripura himself; / Somanātha residing at the pool of tigers was not beheld;
Ghusṛṇeśa, the god residing at Revāpura, was not seen; / Nāganātha renowned in Nāgadantapura was not beheld;
the great Amṛteśvara residing in Parṇagrāma was not seen; / Harihara himself residing on the bank of the Tungabhadrā was not seen;
Śrīnivāsa dwelling on Mount Veṅkaṭa was not contemplated; / Śrīraṅga on the bank of the pericarp of the Kāverī was not beheld;
the miserable and helpless, crying out, were not released from prison; / living creatures were not honored with gifts of food during famine;
no water station was set up anywhere, night after night, in a waterless tract;
no bath was taken in the Gautamī, nor was Hariṇeśvara seen; / no bath was taken in the Kṛṣṇaveṇī when Jupiter entered Virgo;
not even a piece of land was given, nor were poets honored; / no sacrificial session was performed at holy places, nor were sacrifices made in villages;
no large reservoirs full of water were made along the middle of the road; / nor were temples built anywhere for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the wielder of Pināka;
never were those overcome with fear who had fled for refuge protected! / How has this god-given [status] been acquired here by a single merit?”
Becoming anxious in this manner, Purandara, to ask Hari, / went swiftly and dejectedly to the hollow of the milk ocean.
Entering there, he addressed Govinda, who was reclining in sleep, with new hymns of praise, / and spoke of the sorrow of the sudden loss of his sovereignty.
Indra said: / “O beloved of Ramā, in former times a hundred sacrifices were performed for your pleasure; / by that merit the status of Indra was attained by me.
Now a certain new Indra has arisen in heaven; / no religious duty was performed by him, nor were any sacrifices made.
How has my divine throne been occupied, O Acyuta?”
Mahādeva said: / Hearing the words of him who was speaking thus, the Lord of Ramā / opened his smiling eyes and spoke sweet words.
The Holy One said: / “What use are gifts bearing little fruit? What use are austerities? What use are sacrifices? / Living on the surface of the earth, he formerly pleased me.”
Indra said: / “O Lord, by what action did that twice-born please you, / out of delight in which the Lord gave him the status of Indra?”
The Holy One said: / “In the eighteenth chapter of the Gītā he recited five verses; / by that merit your excellent sovereignty was attained.
Become steadfast through that which has become the crest-jewel of all merits.” / Hearing this speech of Viṣṇu, Indra, knowing the means,
assumed the disguise of a brāhmaṇa and went to the bank of the Godāvarī. / There he saw the holy, excellent town named Kālikāgrāma,
where the god Kāleśvara, the crusher of death, resides. / There on the bank of the Godāvarī, he saw a most righteous,
compassionate brāhmaṇa, thoroughly versed in the Vedas, / of restrained mind, who daily recited the eighteenth chapter.
Then, rolling at his two feet with supreme joy, / he recited the eighteenth chapter taught by him.
Then, by that merit, abandoning the petty status of Indra and the other gods, / he attained intimate union with Viṣṇu.
Filled with supreme joy upon attaining knowledge, he went to the city of Vaikuṇṭha. / Therefore, this is indeed the supreme, highest truth of the sages.
The divine glorification of eighteen chapters has been narrated by me, / hearing which alone one is released from all sins.
Thus has been recounted the glorification of the Gītā, which destroys sin, / meritorious, pure, longevity-giving, leading to heaven, and a great blessing.
The person, O noble one, who hears it endowed with faith, / having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, attains union with Viṣṇu.

6.193.m: Pārvatī said: / O God of gods, Mahādeva, omniscient one, bestower of all purposes! / Having shown supreme compassion to me, tell me that which I ask.
The glorification of the Gītā, containing many wondrous stories, has been heard; / by that, devotion has arisen in me to hear the supreme story of Kṛṣṇa.
Among all the Purāṇas, the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is supreme, / wherein Kṛṣṇa is sung in many ways at every step by the sages; / tell now its glorification in truth, together with its legendary history.
Īśvara said: / In Naimiṣa, having saluted Sūta of great intelligence as he was seated, / Śaunaka, skilled in tasting the nectar-essence of the stories, spoke:
Śaunaka said: / Dispersing the darkness of ignorance, destroying the sins of millions of births,
the narrative of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, O Sūta, recount as an elixir! / How does discrimination, rich in devotion, knowledge, and dispassion, grow?
And how is the dispelling of great delusion accomplished by the Vaiṣṇavas? / Here in the terrible Kali [age], the living being has largely become demonic.
What is the elixir for purifying that [soul] afflicted with afflictions? / What is the supreme good among supreme goods, and the purifier of purifiers,
and the means that produces delight for Kṛṣṇa—tell that now! / The wish-fulfilling jewel [gives] worldly happiness; [generosity grants] the wealth of the abode of the lord of the gods;
a pleased guru gives Vaikuṇṭha, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Sūta said: / Pleased, I shall narrate to you, O best among the twice-born, just as I heard, / that which is the essence of essences, and which destroys the fear of worldly existence,
that which causes devotion to increase and is the cause of Kṛṣṇa's satisfaction. / Listen attentively, O virtuous one, as I tell it.
Providing protection to the world licked by the mouth of the serpent of Time, / the scripture of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata was spoken in the Kali [age] by Kṛṣṇa.
There is indeed nothing else besides this that purifies the mind; / it is obtained by the virtuous through merits performed in other lives.
Knowing the liberation of King Parīkṣit, the lotus-born [Brahmā] / weighed the scriptures and the great Purāṇas;
the Śrīmad Bhāgavata was found heavier on earth. / The message of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is difficult to attain even for the gods.
Having reflected thus in many ways, the sages, virtuous and spotless, / considered the glorious Bhāgavata to be the very form of the Lord on earth.
From reading or hearing it, a man goes to the abode of Hari. / Hearing it for a year gives much happiness;
in a month, one attains the dawn of devotion, O best of the twice-born; / and heard in seven days, it grants liberation in every way.
What need of much speaking, O virtuous one? The nectar of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, / which reveals the divine play of Kṛṣṇa, should be drunk constantly by the good.
Formerly it was told by Sanaka and the others, full of compassion, to Nārada, / who had previously heard [it] from Brahmā, as the rule for hearing it in seven days.
Śaunaka said: / Having obtained the supreme knowledge called the Śrīmad Bhāgavata from his father, / Nārada, who knows the reality of the world, wanders the earth at all times.
Where did the meeting of Nārada with those great souls take place, / where the rule for hearing [it] in seven days was heard by the divine sage?
Sūta said: / Here I shall describe to you a story endowed with devotion, / which formerly was told to me by the compassionate Brahmarāta.
Once in Viśālā, Sanaka and the others saw / Nārada seated, his face cast down, his mind dejected.
Seeing their brother, the divine sage, absorbed in thought, / the sages, contemplators of reality, filled with wonder, asked:
The Kumāras said: / Why are you anxious, O holy one, exceedingly dejected as if distressed? / This is not fitting for you whose company is liberation; tell the reason.
Nārada said: / I came to the earth, knowing it to be the best of the best, / endowed with various kinds of holy places, bestowing merit, the embodiment of merit.
At Puṣkara, at Prayāga, at Kāśī, on the bank of the Godāvarī, / in Harikṣetra, in Kurukṣetra, at Śrīraṅga, at Setubandha—
wandering here and there among these and other holy places, / I did not see anywhere happiness that causes satisfaction to the mind.
Now this earth is afflicted by Kali, the enemy of dharma; / truth, purity, compassion, and charity are nowhere on the surface of the earth.
People are belly-fillers, wretched, false witnesses, / sluggish, of very dull intellect, taking refuge in great heresy.
Householders are dominated by women, and members of the castes are devoid of vows; / forest dwellers reside in towns, and renouncers are intent on sense pleasures.
They sell daughters out of greed; they are devoted to agricultural labor; / of fallen conduct, hypocritical, displaying self-willed behavior.
Hermitages are blocked by Yavanas, and holy places, rivers, and lakes; / and temples of the deities here have been destroyed by the wicked.
No yogin, accomplished adept, man of knowledge, or person of good deeds is seen here; / today spiritual practice has turned to ashes by the forest fire of Kali.
Communities have commerce for stakes, twice-born men have Śiva for stakes, / and women have their hair for stakes—such are seen everywhere on earth.
Once I arrived at the auspicious bank of the Yamunā; / there Vṛndāvana was seen, where the divine play of Hari took place.
And what wonder was seen there, let that be heard, O lords of sages! / A young woman was seated there, her mind distressed.
Two old men, fallen beside her, were sighing, unconscious; / serving them, awakening them, she was weeping before the two of them.
Glancing in all directions as if looking for her protector, / being fanned by many women, being consoled again and again.
Seeing her from afar, I went near her out of curiosity; / seeing me, that young woman stood up and spoke these words:

The young woman said: / O virtuous one, stay here for a moment and remove my anxiety! / The sight of such men, O gentle one, removes the multitude of all sins; / by past merit alone does one obtain your sight.
Thus addressed by her, I, my mind softened with compassion, / asked that fair-limbed woman, stirred by curiosity:
Who are you, and who are these two, O gentle one? And who are these lotus-eyed women? / Tell before me everything, the cause of your sorrow.
Questioned thus by me, that young woman, distressed in mind, / related all the grief and the cause of her grief.
The young woman said: / I am known as Bhakti; these two excellent ones are my sons, / named Jñāna and Vairāgya, worn out by the effect of Time.
And these rivers, Gaṅgā and the others, have come for the sake of serving me; / though served by them constantly with respect, O Nārada,

Yet I obtain no good whatsoever and am exhausted in every way, O sage.
Hear my former story, O best of Brahmins,

whereby I became sorrowful and find happiness nowhere.
I was born in Drāviḍa and grew up in Karṇāṭaka;

I resided for a little while in Mahārāṣṭra, and became decrepit in Gurjara.
There, through the onset of the terrible Kali age, my limbs were mangled by heretics,
and I, along with my two sons, became weak and dull for a long time.

Having reached this Vṛndāvana by the working of destiny, O Nārada,
I became a young girl again, appearing as if newly made and beautiful.

These two, however, my sons, lie here distressed in mind.
Leaving aside these two who are extremely aged, I am not able to go now.

How have I become a young girl, and why are my sons old?
When the three of us are of one nature, whence has this inversion arisen?

It is fitting that the mother be old and the two sons be young.
Therefore I grieve for myself, my mind filled with wonder.

If you know, O knower of dharma, compassionate protector of the poor,
tell me everything just as it truly is, and whatever the cause here may be.

Being thus questioned by her, and having reflected for a moment,
I spoke, addressing Devotion, who had been afflicted for a long time:

Through knowledge I perceive all of your story, O sinless one.
Do not despair, O wise woman; Hari will bring you peace.

O young girl, this dreadful Kali age robs all living beings of vitality;
by it good conduct, the path of yoga, and austerities have been destroyed.
And people, committing deceit and wickedness, behave like Aghāsura and demons; / the virtuous in this world are afflicted with great sorrow, while the unrighteous are joyful in mind.

No one whose mind is firm is seen, not even a learned man;
and this earth, agitated by the burden of the wicked, is unfit to be seen or touched.

Gradually, year by year, auspiciousness decreases day by day.
No one looks upon you, O lady, nor upon these two sons of yours.

Abandoned by those full of passion, you have grown decrepit;
[yet] from contact with Vṛndāvana, you have become a young girl again.

And blessed is this Vṛndāvana, where Devotion has become fresh [and young];
for lack of anyone to accept them here, these two have not attained youthfulness.

They seem to be asleep here with a little happiness of their own.
Devotion said:
Why was impure Kali permitted to remain by King Parīkṣit?
Why was unrighteousness neglected by Hari, who is full of compassion?

Dispel this doubt of mine; I am made happy by your words.
Having heard her words, I spoke once more, O twice-born:

If I am asked by you, O young girl, listen with love.
When the blessed Mukunda left the earth and went to his own abode,

from that day Kali, the obstructor of truth, became active.
Seen by the king during his conquest of the quarters, he took refuge like a helpless wretch.

He was not killed, as [the king] saw his virtue; but this is common to all:
Whatever fruit is not attained through austerity, nor through yoga, nor through absorption,

that fruit a wise person attains in the Kali age by reciting the praises of Keśava.
Seeing that Kali is of such a nature, bestowing the fruit of fruits that is the essence,

Viṣṇurāta established him for the welfare of those born in the Kali age.
Through the practice of bad deeds, the essence has now departed on every side;

things remain on earth like chaff without grain.
Through Brahmins the story of the Bhāgavata in house after house and person to person

was caused to be performed out of greed for wealth; therefore the essence of the story was lost.
Fierce in many deeds, people who are atheists and hypocrites

remain at all the pilgrimage sites; therefore the essence of pilgrimage sites was lost.
Those whose minds are agitated by desire, anger, great greed, and craving

undertake ritual actions; therefore the essence of actions was lost.
And from lack of restraint of the mind, from greed, ostentation, and reliance on heresy,

as well as from not studying the scriptures, the fruit of meditation and yoga was lost.
Those learned men delight in their wives like buffaloes;

they are skilled in producing sons, but not skilled in the means to liberation.
Indeed, nowhere is there devotion to Viṣṇu following traditional lineage;

all are intent on reviling the gods, devoted to reviling holy men.
Yet this is the duty of the cosmic age; whose fault is it said to be?
Therefore, remembering the lotus-eyed one, you will attain happiness.

Having heard these words spoken by me, she was filled with wonder,
and praising me, spoke again, O best of the twice-born:

Devotion said:
O divine sage, you are indeed blessed; through my good fortune you have arrived.
The sight of holy men in this world bestows all accomplishments.

Now indicate to me, O sage, how there may be an easy means [to relief].
For you, who know all, O Brahmin, nothing indeed is unachievable in this world.

Through merely understanding a single arrangement of your words, Dhruva conquered unconquered Māyā, and through whose grace Dhruva indeed attained the firm status—to that son of Brahmā, who is a shelter, I bow.

6.194.m:
Sūta said:
Being thus petitioned by that Devotion who was extremely miserable, O Brahmins,
listen, O compassionate ones, to what he indeed told her.

Nārada said:
Do not grieve in vain, O young girl; fixing your mind in your heart,
remember the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and you will obtain happiness.

That Kṛṣṇa by whom Draupadī was rescued from the outrage of the Kauravas,
and by whom the beautiful cowherd maidens were protected, has not gone anywhere.

You are indeed Devotion, dearer to him always than his own breath of life.
When invoked by you, the Blessed Lord goes even to the houses of the lowborn.

In the three cosmic ages beginning with the Kṛta age, knowledge and detachment brought about liberation;
but in the Kali age, pure devotion alone brings about union with Brahman.
Having decided thus, he whose nature is consciousness, the embodiment of supreme bliss and consciousness, / created you from his own limb, his beloved, with a pleased mind.

Having folded your hands, Hari was asked by you, 'What shall I do?'
Kṛṣṇa then commanded you: 'Nourish my devotees.'

That was accepted by you, and Hari was pleased then;
he gave you Liberation as a maidservant, and Knowledge and Detachment as sons.

Remaining in Vaikuṇṭha, you constantly nourish devotees;
and on earth, you have taken the form of a shadow to nourish devotees.

Indeed, you came here together with Liberation, Knowledge, and Detachment;
from the Kṛta age to the end of the Dvāpara age, Liberation remained in joy.

Treating these two as sons, you have kept them protected by your side;
neglected in the Kali age, your two sons have become dull and old.

Nevertheless, abandon worry; I am thinking of a means.
There is no cosmic age equal to Kali, O fair-faced lady;

in it I shall make you renowned in house after house and person to person,
setting aside other duties and giving precedence to great festivals.

If I do not make you flourish, then I am not Hari's servant.
And whatever living beings shall be endowed with you here in Kali,

even though sinners, they will go fearlessly to Hari's abode.
Those in whose minds there is devotion, always in the form of love,

those of pure forms do not see Yama even in a dream;
neither a departed spirit, nor a piśāca, nor a rākṣasa, nor even an asura [approaches them].
The Lord is found in the touch and sight of those whose minds are endowed with devotion, / not by ascetic practices, nor by the Vedas, nor by knowledge, nor by ritual action.
For Hari is attained through devotion; the cowherd women are the proof of that. / Through a thousand births of meritorious people devotion arises.
In the Kali age devotion [alone rules], in the Kali age devotion [alone rules]; through devotion Kṛṣṇa stands before [one]. / Those who act maliciously towards devotion languish in the three worlds.
Durvāsas came to grief in ancient times because he reproached devotion. / Enough with virtuous conduct, enough with holy places, enough with yogas, enough with sacrifices!
Enough with discourses and conversations about knowledge! Devotion alone gives liberation. / When I said this, she indeed, having heard her own glorification,
filled with joy in all her limbs, spoke a word again to me: / 'Ah, Nārada, you are blessed! Your affection for me is unwavering.
I shall never abandon your mind which has become joined to me. / Through you who are compassionate, O virtuous one, my affliction is destroyed instantly.
My two sons have no consciousness; awaken these two for me!' / Having heard those words of hers, I indeed, filled with compassion,
set about to awaken them, touching them with my hand, / stroking their faces, and loudly uttering a sound into their ears:
'O Knowledge, wake up quickly! O Detachment, wake up!' / And with the sounds of the Vedas and Upaniṣads, and repeated recitations of the Gītā,
being awakened then by that, they somehow came to consciousness. / Not looking with their eyes, yawning, both of them languid,
with grey hair like a crane's, their limbs resembling dry wood, / emaciated with hunger, having merely opened their eyes, they returned to sleep again.
Then I became filled with worry: 'What must be done by me? / Ah, how will their sleep depart, and their extreme old age?'
Thinking thus, remembering Govinda, I sat, O best of the twice-born. / Just then an incorporeal voice spoke: 'Do not grieve, O sage!
Your effort will surely bear fruit, of this there is no doubt. / For this purpose, O divine sage, perform a good deed.
Virtuous men adorned with goodness will tell you of that deed. / When that good deed is performed, their sleep and their old age
will vanish in an instant, and devotion will spread everywhere.' / Although hearing this clear voice from the sky, O twice-born,
I did not understand what the heavenly voice described in secret. / 'What is that deed by which these two will become endowed with knowledge?
Where will those virtuous men be? How will they speak of the good deed? / What is to be done here by me, as spoken by the sky's utterance?'
Then, having left those two there, I went out, O twice-born, / from Vṛndāvana, and asked the best of the twice-born wherever they were.
Then having heard the entire account, their minds amazed, / they did not give any answer, being unfamiliar with the words of the sky.
Some said it was impossible, others that it was incomprehensible, / while others became mute, pondering again and again.
'When awakened repeatedly by the sounds of the Vedas and Upaniṣads and recitations of the Gītā, / that triad did not arise; ah, destiny!
When even by the yogin Nārada it is not known himself, / then how can it be accomplished by other mortal men here?' / Then, afflicted with anxiety, I went to the forest of Badarī.

'I shall perform asceticism right here for that purpose'—so resolved, / in the meantime I saw before me Sanaka and the other lordly sages, / shining like ten million suns, and I spoke to those best among sages:
'Now, through great good fortune, the sight of you has occurred. / Therefore, O greatly fortunate ones, tell the remedy, with pleased minds!
You are the best of yogins, wise, and deeply learned, / Kumāras indeed of five years, and the elders of our ancestors,
always residing in Vaikuṇṭha, intent on singing the praise of Hari, / intoxicated by the nectar-like talk of his playful deeds, devoted to the remembrance of Hari.
Therefore indeed the daughter of Time does not afflict you at all, / by whose mere knit of the brow the two doorkeepers of Hari formerly,
having become demons for three births, returned to that place again. / What was stated by the incorporeal voice? Tell me, what is that means?

How and where it should be performed, let the compassionate ones proclaim, / so that happiness arises for Devotion, Knowledge, and Detachment, / and your renown may be throughout all worlds; tell it fully, O wise ones!'
The Kumāras said: / 'Do not worry, O divine sage; bring joy into your own mind! / A remedy easily accomplished exists here, which gives happiness to all.
Ah, Nārada, you are blessed, the crest-jewel of the detached, / the foremost among the vessels of love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the best among speakers!
It is no wonder in you, O divine sage, who are intent upon the practice of devotion; / it is proper for the servants of Kṛṣṇa to propagate devotion on earth.
Many means have been devised in the world by the sages for attainment, / and they are all accomplished with effort, mostly giving heaven as their fruit.
The path leading to Vaikuṇṭha remains hidden in the worlds; / a virtuous person who teaches it is obtained mostly by good fortune.
That good deed which was pointed out to you by the sky's utterance, O lord of sages, / that should be known here by the omniscient ones of old as the sacrifice of knowledge.
The discourse on the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is the sacrifice of knowledge spoken by Śuka; / it appears to us as giving happiness to Devotion, Knowledge, and Detachment.
All these evils of the Kali age, terrified of the sound of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, / will flee to destruction like wolves from the roar of a lion.
Devotion, accompanied by knowledge and detachment, bearing the essence of love, / will make delightful sport in every house and for every person.'
Sūta said: / Having heard what was said by the Kumāras, Nārada, pleased in mind, / spoke again, pondering its excellence, the venerable one.
Nārada said: / 'Though awakened by the sounds of the Vedas and Upaniṣads and recitations of the Gītā, / that triad did not arise, suppressed by the evils of the Kali age.
How will it attain awakening here from the discourse of the Bhāgavata? / Cut away this doubt, for you are beings of unfailing vision.
Delay should not be made here, O you who are affectionate to those who take refuge!' / Thereupon those Sanaka and the others, detached, their semen drawn up,
perfected, eternal, O twice-born, spoke to Nārada with respect.
The Kumāras said: / 'From the essence of the Vedas and Upaniṣads the story of the Bhāgavata arose; / therefore it shines as the highest, the exalted state of the fruit brought out separately.
Just as the juice of the mango tree exists from root to top, yet in the fruit / it becomes separated through drinking as something charming to the whole world;
just as ghee present in milk is not regarded as tasty [by itself], / but separated, it is divine, increasing the delight of the gods;
and just as sugar stays pervading sugarcanes from beginning to middle and end, / but when separated is sweet—so is the story of the Bhāgavata.
The Purāṇa named Śrīmad Bhāgavata is indeed aesthetic essence itself, / manifested for the happiness of Devotion, Knowledge, and Detachment.
It was manifested by Kṛṣṇa to Brahmā situated in the navel-lotus, through the heart; / those four verses in their entirety appear as the very absolute.
And it was spoken to you by Brahmā as an illustration of his deeds; / by you too it was spoken to Vyāsadeva for the removal of his distress,
by remembering which the son of Bādarāyaṇa, immediately despondent, / composed the great narrative charming to those who delight in the self.'
Why is there any wonder in you about this, that you should ask again and again? / The scripture of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is capable of drawing Kṛṣṇa near.

Sūta said: / Hearing this desired statement uttered by the lords of yogins, the foremost among whom was Sanaka, / [Nārada], joyful, clasped their feet with devotion, bowed with his head, and spoke to those dispellers of worldly distress:

Nārada said: / The very sight of you destroys a flood of sins and expands the welfare of those afflicted by the forest fire of worldly suffering. / Merely by drinking the narrative sung by the mouths of Śeṣa without remainder, I have taken refuge in you to manifest love [for Hari].

When, through the rising of merit gathered across many births, association with the virtuous occurs for a fortunate man, / then the great darkness of delusion caused by ignorance is destroyed, and indeed great discernment arises.

6.195.m: Thus, in the holy Padma Purāṇa, in the fifty-five-thousand-verse compendium, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the glorification of the glorious Bhāgavata, the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter.
The Kumāras said: / Listen, Nārada! We shall tell you where the narrative of men / who hear it destroys heaps of sins and increases merit.
Sūta said: / When they had thus sat down, Bhṛgu and the others according to their rank, / they declared the glorification of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata to Nārada.

On the full-moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, adorned on a golden lion throne, / one should present the Śrīmad Bhāgavata to a foremost twice-born.

Endowed with supreme compassion, gave him the Bhāgavata; / having deposited his own brilliance into the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, O twice-born,
The Blessed Lord, having given it to Uddhava, entered his own abode. / Therefore, this embodiment of speech belonging to the auspicious Hari exists here.
From constantly venerating it, the sins of men are destroyed in an instant; / hence the seven-day hearing is declared to be superior to everything else.
The hearer, the speaker, and the inquirer attain oneness with it, O twice-born. / For washing away sorrow, poverty, misfortune, and sin,

And for conquering desire and anger in the Kali age, the Bhāgavata is competent. / Otherwise, how can the Vaiṣṇava māyā, insurmountable even to the gods, / turn away from men without the Śrīmad Bhāgavata?
Sūta said: / Having thus proclaimed the glorification of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, / they set out to recite the divine narrative of the Lord.
As the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, the essence of the Vedas and Upaniṣads, / was being commenced by the twice-born, right there Devotion appeared in an instant,
Endowed with love, possessing a lovely form, and holding with her own two arms her two joyful, youthful sons, / repeatedly uttering the names, 'O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O Govinda, O Hari, O Murāri, O Lord!'

The compassionate [sages] saw her who had arrived, adorned with the meaning of the Bhāgavata and wearing lovely attire; / and with eyes wide in utter astonishment, they all wondered, 'How, whence, and who is this?'

Then the Kumāras, whose purpose was fulfilled, spoke: 'She has now stepped forth out of the meaning of the narrative.' / Hearing these words, she, accompanied by her sons, bowed and addressed the sons of the lotus-born [Brahmā]:

Bhakti said: / By you today I have been nourished through the juice of the narrative, though lost in the Kali age. / Where shall I stay? Point out to me a desirable dwelling place together with these two.

Sūta said: / Hearing her words, the sons of Brahmā, deliberating well and concentrating their minds, / spoke to Bhakti, who removes the illness of worldly existence and bestows love alone upon those devoted to Hari.

The Kumāras said: / In the devotees devoted to Govinda, in the virtuous, and in those dedicated to compassion for the wretched, / restraining the mind from running astray and making it single-pointed upon Hari's lotus feet—
Then indeed these defects born of the Kali age, though powerful in the world, cannot look upon you. / In the Kali age, you alone, presented by Nārada, will be for the welfare of the world.

In all the worlds, even the poor are exceedingly blessed in whose heart alone dwells the devotion to Śrī Hari; / even Hari quickly leaves his own realm and enters the heart of those bound by the cord of love.

6.196.m: Sūta said: / Then, beholding extraordinary devotion in the hearts of the Vaiṣṇavas, / Hari abandoned his own realm and came to earth.
Wearing a forest garland, dark as a rain-cloud, clad in yellow garments, wearing a crown, / encircled with a girdle and belt, with shining alligator-shaped earrings,
Graceful in his threefold-bending posture, resplendent with the lovely Kaustubha gem, / possessing the beauty of ten million gods of love, anointed with yellow sandalwood paste,
Having an embodiment of consciousness that is supreme bliss, charming, holding a flute, / he entered the pure hearts of his own devotees.
And those Vaiṣṇavas residing in Vaikuṇṭha whose minds were tranquil / arrived in disguised form in order to hear the stories of Hari.
Then there arose a loud cry of 'Victory, victory!' accompanied by the blast of conches, / by which the terrible inauspiciousness born of the Kali age dissolved.
And seeing that the people gathered there forgot their homes and bodies, / Nārada, who knows the truth of the supreme Self, spoke to the Kumāras:
Nārada said: / O lords of sages, this extraordinary greatness arising from the seven-day [recitation] has been witnessed by me today.
Even those who are foolish, wicked, or beasts and birds, go to the supreme state; / therefore, in the human realm, no other pure scripture has been ordained for purifying the mind.

Which destroys the flood of sins and brings about fulfillment in the Kali age, the ocean of faults. O Kumāras, / tell me: by what means do which [people] become purified through the seven-day sacrificial rite consisting of the narrative?
