6.196.m: By you who are compassionate and intent on the world's welfare, an unprecedented path has been revealed. / The Kumāras said: / Those men who are perpetrators of sin, exceedingly wicked, constantly delighting in bad conduct, and envious,
Consumed by the fire of anger, crooked, and lustful—they reach Hari by means of the seven-day sacrificial rite.

Those devoid of truth, revilers of their mother and father, overwhelmed by craving, outside the stages of life and castes, / those who are hypocrites and slayers of living beings—they reach Hari by means of the seven-day sacrificial rite.

Those guilty of the five terrible sins, deceitful ones, cruel ones, pitiless as piśācas, / those who fatten themselves on what belongs to Brahmins, and adulterers—they go to Hari by the seven-day sacrificial session.
Those rogues who obstinately and constantly commit sin with body, speech, and mind, / the vile, the ungrateful, the defiled, and the evil-minded—they go to Hari by the seven-day sacrificial session.
Sūta said: / Now, when Nārada, who is worshiped by the gods, was thus satisfied in heart, / those delighted Kumāras spoke once more to Nārada.
The Kumāras said: / In this regard we will recount to you an ancient legendary history, / by the mere hearing of which destruction of sin is brought about.
Formerly, on the bank of the Tuṅgabhadrā, in a city named Kohalā, / endowed with the conduct of the castes and life-stages, teeming with wealth and grain,
there lived a best of Brahmins known as Ātmadeva, / learned in Vedic knowledge and ritual rules, devoted to daily rites.
His beloved wife was named Dhuṃdhulī, constantly devoted to her own self-interest, / bent on asserting her own word, yet beautiful and born of a good family.
Through the ripening of past actions, she was mostly a big chatterbox, / clever in household chores, but cruel and fond of quarrel.
As that couple lived there without offspring, / their age even passed the measure of fifty years.
Then, dwelling in the house without offspring, the two became sorrowful. / For the sake of producing progeny, wealth and the like was given by both of them.
Cows, lands, gold, and garments were given, and many [other things]; / yet on account of past actions, neither a son nor a daughter was born.
And once, despondent, that best of Brahmins, Ātmadeva, / abandoned his home and went to the forest, sorrowful because of childlessness.
Wandering here and there, bewildered, with his mind distressed by grief, / emaciated by hunger and seized by thirst, by chance he reached a reservoir of water.
Having drunk water at that pond, that best of Brahmins / sat down under the shade of a tree, O Nārada.
Then, just at that moment, a certain perfected yogin wandering the earth came there. / He too, having drunk water at the pond, arrived at that very place.
Seeing that tranquil ascetic, the noble-minded Ātmadeva / rose, honored him, and grasped his feet as if those of his own guru.
Then the two sat down, asked questions of each other, / and became very affectionate in mind, like guru and disciple in a hermitage.
Then that ascetic, seeing him sighing and grieving inside, / an ocean of compassion, questioned Ātmadeva standing before him.
The perfected yogin said: / What worry resides in your heart, causing sorrow, O best of Brahmins? / Declare that tormenting [worry] to me, O knower of dharma.
Hearing that speech of that great-souled perfected yogin, / Ātmadeva then explained the cause of his sorrow.
Ātmadeva said: / What shall I say, O sage, of the sorrow accumulated by past actions? / My ancestors partake only of lukewarm water [at libations].
The ancestors and the deities do not accept the offering given by me. / Despondent because of that sorrow, I have come here to cast off my life.
A life devoid of progeny is cursed, and cursed are the home, the wealth, and the lineage. / Even the cow that is maintained by me turns out to be barren.
Even the tree that is planted by me becomes barren. / What is the use of my life, being unfortunate and childless?
The Kumāras said: / Having spoken thus, he wept aloud before him, afflicted by grief. / At that, great compassion arose in the heart of the ascetic.
And seeing and discerning the lines written on his forehead, that wise master of yoga / spoke again at length to the Brahmin Ātmadeva.
The perfected yogin said: / Listen, O Brahmin, today your destiny has been examined by me: / no attainment of a son is seen, up to the limit of seven births.
Abandon your insistence for the sake of progeny; the course of past action is very strong. / Attaining discernment, be happy, O noble-minded one.
Hearing this speech of the perfected yogin, the best of Brahmins, / his mind bound to the hope of progeny, spoke to the perfected yogin, exceedingly grieved.
The Brahmin said: / What will come of discernment for me? Give me a son even by force; / otherwise, fainting from grief, I shall give up my life before you.
Seeing the brāhmaṇa's persistence, that ascetic said: / "Sagara obtained grief from offspring, as did Aṅga, the lord of creatures.
Citraketu came to distress through rubbing out the decree of fate. / Therefore, O knower of dharma, even if you were to obtain a son,
you would not be happy with a son; fate is indeed more powerful.” / Having said this to the best of Brahmins, that perfected yogin, honored by the virtuous,
gave a fruit to him who was seeking a son with insistence: / “This fruit is given by me to you for obtaining a son, O Brahmin.
Give it to your wife; a son will be born to you, without doubt. / Truthfulness, purity, compassion, giving, and eating only one meal a day—
must be observed by the woman for a year; by that, the son will become pure.” / Having spoken thus, the yogin departed, and the Brahmin went to his home.
Having given that fruit to his wife, he spoke what was said by the perfected yogin. / Then the cruel Dhuṃdhulī, eager to assert her own word,
told her female friend everything spoken by her husband and uttered by the perfected yogin: / “If I were to eat this fruit offered by the perfected yogin,
then pregnancy would occur in me, and how could I endure it? / I would have little food, and weakness in walking and in household duties.

If the fetus were to come out transverse, then my death would occur. / In childbirth there is terrible pain; how can I, being delicate, endure it? / If I were incapacitated, my sister-in-law would constantly seize all my possessions.
Anxiety has overtaken me; what shall I do, O woman of radiant smile?” / Hearing her words, out of fear of breaking their affection, O Brahmin,
she with a smiling face said to her with affection: “It is just so!” / Thus, through poor reasoning, that fruit was not eaten at all.
When asked by her husband, “Was the fruit eaten?”, she declared, “It was eaten.” / One day, her sister came to her house of her own accord.
Before her, everything was told: “This is a great worry to me here; / what shall I do? I am pregnant; tell me as it truly is.”
She said: “A child is in my womb; I will give it to you after delivery. / For that long, remain happily concealed in your house as though pregnant.
I will nourish that boy in your house constantly. / Give the fruit to a cow today for the sake of a test, O woman of fair face.”

Having spoken thus, she went to her own house with a joyful heart; / and as she was instructed by Dhundhulī, her sister acted accordingly.

Then, having given birth, she quickly handed the child over to Dhundhulī, / and she told her husband: 'A child has safely been born.'
Happiness arose among the people at the rise of Ātmadeva's offspring. / Giving gifts to the best of Brahmins, he also performed the birth-rites.
There was the sound of singing and musical instruments, an utmost auspiciousness in his house. / The noble-minded Ātmadeva attained joy.
Then she said to her husband: “There is no milk in my breasts; / how shall I nourish the newborn boy now, O lord?
When my sister gave birth formerly, her child died. / Bringing her, keep her in the house; she will nourish the child.”
Hearing these words of Dhundhulī, that best of the twice-born, / the deluded Ātmadeva, did precisely that, filled with joy.
His mother properly gave him the name Dhundhukāri. / That son of his mother’s sister was constantly nourished with [her] milk.
And when three months had passed, that cow gave birth to a child, / handsome in every limb, divine, spotless, and radiant like gold.
Seeing him, the brahmin was delighted and performed the sacraments himself. / All the people, desiring to see him, arrived in utter astonishment:
“By the rise of great good fortune of Ātmadeva the brahmin, / a child of godlike form has been born to a cow—what a great wonder!”
Through the working of fate, that secret was not known to anyone. / Seeing his son [with cow-ears], Gokarna named him Gokarna.
After some time, both of them reached youth: / Gokarna was a learned and wise man, while Dhundhukāri was a great scoundrel.
Lacking rites of bathing and purification, eating edible and inedible things alike, overflowing with anger, / a thief, hating all people, consorting with wicked caṇḍālas,
he would seize playing children by force and throw them into a well. / In this way, through attachment to courtesans, he brought his father’s wealth to ruin.
His father, impoverished with grief like a wretched man, wept: / “A childless man is ever happy; a wicked son brings only sorrow.
The word spoken by the perfected sage is true; I have now experienced it. / Where shall I go? Where shall I stay? Who will dispel my misery?
I shall abandon my life-breaths in water, in fire, or cast myself from a precipice!” / While he was thus lamenting with downcast face, he was approached
by the wise Gokarna, who enlightened his father concerning reality: / Gokarna said: “Dear father, this transmigratory existence is worthless; it brings sorrow and delusion to mortals.
Who is a son? What is wealth? Whose is it? Who is a wife? Who is a husband, father? / Bound by delusion, the wretched soul of man suffers, not otherwise.
There is no happiness for Indra, nor any happiness for a universal monarch; / happiness belongs to the detached sage who is devoted to solitude, dear father.
Cast off the ignorance in the form of progeny—a delusion that causes hell. / Free from dualities, free from pride, abandon everything and go to the forest.”
Then, hearing that statement, that brahmin said to Gokarna: / The brahmin said: “Explain to me in detail, virtuous one, what is to be done in the forest.
For I am bound by the noose of delusion, roguish, of a miserable mind, / fallen into the pit of worldly existence: deliver me, ocean of compassion!”
Hearing this word of his father, Gokarna, learned in wisdom, / spoke to his wretched and dejected father with a joyful mind.

Gokarna said: / “In this body of yours, a mere heap of flesh, bones, and blood, quickly abandon ownership and possessiveness toward wife, sons, and the rest. / See this world constantly as subject to momentary destruction; become a wise man, savoring detachment, devoted to loving devotion.

Ever practice dharma, abandon worldly ways, revere holy men, renounce desire and craving; / quickly giving up pondering the faults and merits of others, drink abundantly of the sweet nectar of the story of Viṣṇu.”

The Kumāras said: / Having thus realized the experience spoken by his son, free from desire, having abandoned his house, firm in mind, at the age of sixty, / constantly following the people dear to Hari, that great-souled man, dwelling in the forest, attained the hard-to-reach abode of Hari.

6.197.m: The Kumāras said: / When his father had thus reached the forest, Dhundhukāri, the great rogue, / coming afterward, threatened his mother, Nārada:
“Tell me, where does the wealth lie?” [he said] to his mother, Nārada; / “I will certainly kill you if you do not tell me of the treasure!”
Terrified by his words, her mind anguished at night, / she fell into a well and died; when people discovered it, she was pulled out.
After Gokarna cremated her with the brahmins and her kinsmen and relatives, / the wise man, regarding sorrow and happiness as equal, set out on a pilgrimage to sacred places, O sage.
Dhundhukāri, staying at his own house surrounded by courtesans, / his intellect utterly deluded in maintaining them through exceedingly cruel deeds and conduct—
desiring ornaments, the courtesans said to him: / “O beloved, all of us have joined with you as our protector,
and remain here; there is no other giver of wealth, O honor-giver! / Therefore, fine clothes and radiant ornaments
give us; otherwise, we shall depart from you to another man.” / Hearing their words and reflecting for a moment, he
went out from his house at night, blinded by lust and not thinking of death; / stealing clothes and ornaments from someone’s house,
he gave them to them with joy and affection, O Nārada. / But seeing those priceless clothes and ornaments,
those women thought, “These have been brought by him through theft!” / Resolving this, they deliberated among themselves:
“He continually commits theft; the king will seize him. / Having confiscated the wealth, he will surely execute him.
Therefore, having killed this thief in secret ourselves / and taking much wealth, why shouldn't we go elsewhere?”
Thus those cruel-hearted women, seizing the sleeping one by the throat, / bound him with very sharp ropes and prepared to kill him.
And when he did not die from the severe strangling of his throat, / they then cast many burning charcoals into his mouth.
Agitated by the intense agony of the flame of fire, he met his death. / They threw his body into a pit, for women are mostly daring.
That act was not known to anyone, O best of sages. / When questioned by the people, they said, “Our husband has gone far away;
attracted by wealth, he will return after a long time.” / Therefore, the best of wise men should place no trust in women.
They slay the one who trusts them in every way, ever seeking someone new. / Their speech is made of nectar, increasing the passion of lustful men,
while their heart is like the edge of a razor. Who is truly dear to women? / Then those courtesans, taking abundant wealth,
went swiftly to another village, deeply panicked out of fear of the king. / And Dhundhukāri, the evil-doer, became a great preta.
Assuming the form of a whirlwind, constantly running in all directions due to his bad death, / tormented by cold and heat, deprived of food and thirsty,
he found no happiness anywhere, continually wailing, “Alas, alas!” / After some time, when Gokarna learned that he was dead,
he performed the śrāddha at Gayā while on his pilgrimage to sacred places. / Completing his pilgrimage, he then returned to his own city.
Welcomed with affection by the citizens, his own people, and relatives, / the twice-born dwelt in his own house for some days.
Knowing that Gokarna was asleep at night in the courtyard of the house, / the greatly wicked Dhundhukāri revealed a terrifying form.
In one moment he was an elephant, in one moment a camel, in one moment he became a buffalo; / in one moment fire, in one moment a serpent, and in a moment he became a man.
Seeing this extraordinary reversal, Gokarna, endowed with fortitude / and wise, wondered in astonishment: “What is this?”
"This is some vile person who has fallen into an evil state." / Having thus resolved in his mind, full of compassion, he spoke to him:
Gokarṇa said: / "Who are you, so terrifying, who have approached me in the night to frighten me? / Are you a preta or a piśāca? Whence have you come to this condition?
Speak, then, noble one! What should I do for you now, / since you have approached near me in the night with such a dreadful form?"
Hearing his brother's words, Dhundhukārī, the greatly wicked one / who had attained the state of a ghost, wept, exceedingly tormented.
He was not able to speak with words at all, bewitched by his preta state; / then, being thirsty, he indicated by gesture [that he wanted] water to drink.
Then that highly fortunate Gokarṇa, esteemed by the virtuous, / took water into his hollowed hands and threw it [toward him], uttering [a prayer].
That water thrown by his brother, the great-souled Gokarṇa, / arrived for the satisfaction of the preta Dhuṃdhukārī.
Then, his consciousness restored by that water offered / by his brother Gokarṇa of virtuous soul, O Nārada, he spoke.
The preta said: / "I am your brother, known by the name Dhuṃdhukārī; / through the fault of my own deeds I have fallen into the state of a preta.
My mother died of grief, having been threatened many times by me / for the sake of wealth. Later, eager to maintain courtesans,
I performed forbidden actions, such as theft and the like, out of greed for wealth. / Once, asked by them for ornaments and clothes,
I stole them from the house of a wealthy man at night and brought them [to them]. / Then, out of greed for wealth, having bound my neck by force with ropes,
they killed me by throwing me into fire, O respect-giver! / Having seized my abundant wealth, they all, out of fear of the king,
fled from this city, their friendship uprooted by self-interest. / Thus I entered the state of a preta, O brother! Today, sprinkled with water
by you, a most compassionate, meritorious soul, I have regained consciousness. / I live feeding only on wind, experiencing the fruit ordained by fate.
I saw you, my brother, asleep in the courtyard of your own house; / then, finding you unaware, I made an effort to overpower [you],
all of a sudden, O virtuous one; and now I have been recognized by you. / Friend of the wretched, ocean of compassion, O brother, free me swiftly!
From this state of a preta [liberate me]; you have fulfilled all aims, there is no doubt." / Having heard this speech of his brother, Gokarṇa, wise and possessed of knowledge,
his heart sorrowful, spoke to his suffering brother Dhuṃdhukārī. / Gokarṇa said: "A piṇḍa was offered by me for you at Gayā, after I heard

from the mouths of people, O brother, that you were dead. How have you gone into the state of a preta? / By the offering of a piṇḍa at Gayā, even one fallen into an evil state attains an auspicious destiny;
there is no doubt of this. How have you not gone to heaven?" / Having heard such words of his brother, the great-souled Gokarṇa,
Dhuṃdhukārī, sorrowful at heart, standing before him, spoke: / "Even by a hundred śrāddhas at Gayā my liberation will not happen."
'You must indeed consider another means for my deliverance.' / Hearing his words, Gokarṇa was filled with wonder.
[Gokarṇa] said: "If there is no liberation by śrāddhas, then your destiny is unattainable. / For now, stay in your own place, O preta, free from fear.
Having deliberated, I shall prepare an ultimate means for your liberation." / Hearing these words, Dhuṃdhukārī departed from there
to his own place, a vibhītaka tree standing in a cremation ground, beyond that. / Remaining there, thinking over that night about
his liberation, Gokarṇa did not find a means to it, O Nārada. / Then, at dawn, that Gokarṇa reported the night's event
to his kinsmen, family, relatives, and brāhmaṇas learned in the Dharmaśāstras. / Those twice-born deliberated on that matter extensively in the scriptures,
and when they could not understand that matter, they praised Sūrya. / The twice-born said: "Praise be to you, O maker of light, O Āditya, dispeller of darkness, radiant one!
Witness of the world, abode of the universe, worshipped by gods and asuras, / twelvefold soul, possessor of green steeds, radiant one, awakener of the world!
You are the goal of all the worlds, of those who always practice dharma. / You are Brahmā, you are Hari, you are the trident-bearer, the author of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
Without you there is no refuge for living beings in this world, O omnipresent one! / You are Śarva, having the form of the earth; you are Bhava, bearing the form of water;
you are Rudra, having the form of fire; you are Vāyu, bearing a fierce form; / you are Bhīma, having the sky as your body; you yourself are the sacrificer, Paśupati;
you are Mahādeva, whose form is Soma; and Īśāna is Sūrya indeed! / Your eight divine forms are worshipped by those who profess the Veda
for the fulfillment of all desires, and you pervade the three worlds. / You are the fish supporting the Vedas, and you are the excellent tortoise upholding the mountain;
you are the boar upholding the earth; you are Trivikrama, sustainer of the world; / you are the descendant of Bhṛgu destroying the kṣatriyas; you are Rāghava, subduing the tormentors of the world;
you are Kṛṣṇa, remover of the earth's burden; you are the Buddha, bewildering the asuras; / you are Kalki, slayer of mlecchas, when dharma declines in age after age.
Of gods, asuras, and men, of beasts, birds, and aquatic creatures, / of various kinds of living beings, you are the creator, bearing the form of Brahmā.
You are Indra, you are Dharmarāja, you are Varuṇa, you are the lord of wealth; / you abide in the form of the guardians of the world, O lord of rays and senses!

Embodied as the three Vedas, worshipped at the three junctures of the day, possessing three abodes, composed of the three guṇas, / you alone are worshipped by the worlds, O sun, divided into three forms.

You alone are the awakener of the lotus, O lord of the world!" / As the best of the twice-born, having spoken thus, were standing, O chief of sages,

just then, a voice moving in the sky spoke clearly for them to hear. / The glorious Sūrya said: "Listen, O best of the twice-born, as the best of sages stood,

just then, the sky-goer spoke clearly to them as they listened: / The glorious Sūrya said: "Listen, O best of the twice-born! For the purpose for which I have been praised

For the pacification of the grave sin of Dhundhulī's son by you [all], / through the merit of Ātmadeva, this Gokarṇa was born of a cow.
[conducting] a seven-day reading of the glorious Bhāgavata, will be his savior. / The hymn of praise which was composed by you celebrating my glory—
having praised me with that, a man will attain the path of the gods, O brāhmaṇas! / A seeker of sons, a seeker of wealth, a seeker of dharma, and one desiring liberation,
having recited this hymn, the wish-fulfilling jewel of desires, will attain it completely." / Having spoken thus, the divine sun residing in the sky fell silent.
Those twice-born, their minds rejoiced, said: "Well done!" to Gokarṇa. / Then, in an assembly of brāhmaṇas on the auspicious bank of the Tuṅgabhadrā,
the townspeople came there to witness this very great wonder. / Gokarṇa, who knew the truth of reality, took the seat of the narrator.
Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa and the others, he commenced the seven-day rite. / "The scripture consisting of the words of Śrī Hari, born from his holy lotus-feet—
if it is true, then let the son of Dhuṃdhulī attain a good destiny!" / Having made this resolution in his mind, [the text] named the Śrīmad Bhāgavata,
beginning with "From whom the creation and so on of this [universe] proceed," and ending with "Let us meditate," he recited. / There the preta arrived, looking here and there for a place,
and, assuming the form of wind, entered a bamboo pole with seven joints, / while the brāhmaṇas, foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas, listened, O Nārada.
Dhundhukārin, staying inside the joint's opening, listened day by day. / When the recitation ceased on the first day, O Nārada,
then one bamboo knot burst, and it was indeed a great wonder! / On the second and following days, likewise, occurred the bursting of each single knot.
When the seventh was broken, he immediately discarded the state of a ghost. / Assuming a celestial form, adorned with a garland of tulasī,
clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain-cloud, endowed with ornaments, he shone brightly. / Bowing to his brother Gokarna, the knower of all truth spoke:
“By you, O brother, I have been released out of compassion from the impurity of a ghost. / Blessed is the narrative of the Bhāgavata, the eradicator of ghosthood, which was heard!
Blessed also is the seven-day session, granting entrance to the world of Viṣṇu, / through whose power I, who was intensely tormented, have been freed from the state of a ghost.
Whether wet or dry, small or great, committed by speech, mind, or actions, / sin the seven-day session turns to ashes, as fire does fuel.
In this land of Bhārata, which is desired even by the gods, / for those who listen to the divine scripture, the state attained becomes the most supreme.
A composite of sinews, bones, marrow, flesh, and blood is what is called the body; / it is pure from savoring the Bhāgavata, but otherwise considered impure.
The body polluted by the stain of deeds is a vessel for hell; / therefore, for the cessation of this fault, this alone is indeed the means.
Like bubbles in water, like mosquitoes among creatures, / they are born only to die—those who are bereft of the divine scripture.
The knot of the heart is untied, all doubts are severed, / and his deeds are exhausted when the Bhāgavata is heard, O twice-born ones!”
Even as he was speaking thus, an excellent celestial vehicle arrived / from Vaikuṇṭha; boarding it, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
When he had gone to the world of Viṣṇu, all the best of the twice-born / were astonished in their minds and asked Gokarna:
The twice-born said: / “The Bhāgavata was heard by all of us assembled here; / what is the reason, O fortunate one, that only your brother went to Hari?”
Gokarna said: / “Listen, I shall explain the reason for my brother’s good destination, / hearing which you yourselves will also go to Goloka.
Listening for seven days must be performed by those dedicated to fasting, / with minds solely focused on Kṛṣṇa, which bestows the path to Goloka.
Listen again, O twice-born ones, to the glorious Bhāgavata for seven days / with single-pointed minds, continuously, which bestows the nectar of love for Kṛṣṇa.”
Hearing these words of Gokarṇa, the best of the twice-born / sat together for a week-long session to hear the Bhāgavata once again.
With minds solely focused on Kṛṣṇa and following the rules, O Nārada, / all those twice-born listened again to the glorious Bhāgavata.
At the conclusion of the recitation, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, lotus-eyed, / bearer of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, appeared, O best of sages,
wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with a garland of forest flowers, / clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain-cloud, adorned with bracelets and armlets.
Seeing him accompanied by Viṣvaksena and others, / the foremost attendants, all those twice-born, rejoiced, and bowed together upon the ground.
The sound ‘Victory!’ and the sound ‘Reverence!’ arose on all sides then, O sage; / then Hari blew his conch, delighting the twice-born.
Then many celestial vehicles arrived from Vaikuṇṭha, / filled with foremost attendants, while the twice-born looked on there.
Embracing Gokarna, he gave him his own form; / the other listeners, dark as rain-clouds, dressed in yellow silk,
crowned, wearing earrings, wearing necklaces, bearing garlands of forest flowers, / he made instantly; it was a great wonder there.
Those who lived in that village, down to the cāṇḍālas, O sage, / boarding those celestial vehicles, went to heaven by Kṛṣṇa’s command.

Together with Gokarna, Kṛṣṇa, dear to the cowherds and gopīs, / reached Goloka, situated above all the worlds, / where the delightful Vṛndāvana is, encircled by a hundred peaks.

Surrounded on its outside by Vijayā, it shines exceedingly wondrous; / the forest where there are very many excellent pavilions, clear-water

where the wish-fulfilling cows take refuge in the shade of the celestial tree groves, / and surrounded by cowherd boys whose minds are dedicated to playing, the son of Nanda plays.

In the middle of this beautiful forest, fashioned by the desire of the Lord of Vṛndāvana, / a delightful [tree], illuminating an enclosure studded with a multitude of gems and gold,

A realm unattainable even by severe penances of subsisting on wind, water, and dry leaves, emaciating the body, or by recitation and sacrificial rites, / he who was born of a cow went thither by instituting the sacrifice [of the Bhāgavata].
Whoever reads or even listens to this sacred legendary history / attains even Goloka—what more need be said of the glorious Bhāgavata?
